rv.q: Shadowlands for me wins hands down.
Bonneville certainly deserved the acclaim he received at the end of the evening: this was a shrewdly understated performance

All that genteel restraint means that when Bonneville’s placid, unassuming demeanour breaks into a howl of distress, or his gauche stiffness yields to a kneeling marriage proposal at Joy’s hospital bed, the effect is one of emotional detonation.
Rose-tinted, it all lacks punch; but it’s a heart-warming watch.
Kavanaugh’s pacy staging, bleeding one scene into another, conveys the force of unexpected love but can’t quite overcome these drawbacks.
It’s philosophically interesting and Bonneville and Siff are great as two versions of real people.
Neither this sanitised production nor his unstintingly mild-mannered performance can capture the darker realities of grief, sex and mortality.
But the play’s emotional impact has dulled over the years.
In this production, originally staged at Chichester Festival theatre, it just feels old-fashioned.
I sat totally entranced, as one should do by a really effective piece of drama, and I also found it very profound and moving.
By turns hilarious and deeply affecting, it is a hard heart who could hear Bonneville’s final wail of grief and not want to join in.
This Shadowlands is a thoughtful revival, beautifully performed.
Both actors deliver with light brushstrokes, serving to illuminate their characters' backstories with a playful sensitivity while successfully avoiding any sense of clunking caricature.
Shadowlands is a heartwrenching play that does a brilliant job of balancing warmth and humour, making a genuine emotional impact on the audience.
Its theology and its psychology don’t stand up to too much scrutiny, but like the fruit cake its characters eat over endless teas, it is satisfying while it lasts.
Kavanaugh's direction feels a little pedestrian overall, despite much use of the revolve, but this is a slow-burner of a production. Plodding in parts, but ultimately devastating.
You’ll see better acting at the Edinburgh Fringe but never mind.
Shadowlands is a deeply moving play on life, love, loss, and faith.

cn.t: This old-fashioned but affecting revival of Nicholson's 1989 play earns mixed-to-positive reviews, with Bonneville's warm performance and the moving exploration of love and grief praised, though some find it creaky and overly sentimental.
